text.title: django-models Core Rules
text.summary: Seventeen testable rules for Django domain models: inheritance and thinness, enums and constraints, relationships, indexing, query defaults, validation, and migration hygiene.

rule.statement: Every domain model inherits `BaseModel` (uid + created_at + updated_at, see [[django-base-model]]). `class Foo(models.Model)` is forbidden for a domain entity, and no model redefines `id` / `uid` / the timestamps itself.
rule.rationale: A consistent base is what lets audit trails, uid-only API exposure and soft-delete evolve in one place instead of per model. A model that opts out silently leaks its integer PK the first time it is serialised.

rule.statement: A model carries fields, `Meta`, `__str__`, simple `@property` accessors and pure-self predicates (`is_active`) — nothing else. Cross-model orchestration lives in `services/`, and every service that saves calls `obj.full_clean()` before `obj.save()`.

rationale.source: Two Scoops of Django; Django Model.save docs

rule.rationale: `save()` does NOT call `full_clean()` — only ModelForm and the admin do — so validation written in `clean()` never fires on the service path. And a model method that touches a second model creates a circular dependency that no amount of import trickery fixes.

rule.statement: Status / kind / role / state fields use `TextChoices` (or `IntegerChoices`), defined in the app's `constants.py` and referenced through a module alias: `from apps.users import constants as user_constants` → `choices=user_constants.UserType.choices`. Raw string tuples and docstring-managed values are forbidden.
rule.rationale: `TextChoices` gives `.choices`, `.values`, `.labels`, `.names` and translation hooks from one declaration. Keeping it in `constants.py` is what stops the model, the serializer and the admin from each carrying a slightly different copy of the same list.

rule.statement: Invariants that span more than one field live in `Meta.constraints`: `CheckConstraint` for value ranges, `UniqueConstraint(fields=[...], name="...")` for conditional or composite uniqueness. `unique_together` is forbidden — it is deprecated.
rule.rationale: A DB-level constraint still holds when the ORM is bypassed by `bulk_create`, `update()` or raw SQL, which is exactly when the invariant matters. `unique_together` cannot express a condition and is scheduled for removal.

rule.statement: Every `ForeignKey` and `OneToOneField` declares `on_delete=` deliberately: `PROTECT` for user/account and parent-of-record references, `CASCADE` only when the child row is meaningless without the parent, `SET_NULL` for optional assignees. Each choice carries a reason of at least 10 characters in the spec.

rationale.source: Django 2.0 release notes; production incident history

rule.rationale: Implicit `on_delete` was removed precisely because the old default silently cascaded. `CASCADE` on a user reference turns one account deletion into irreversible loss of everything that account touched.

rule.statement: Domain-specific filter logic lives in `QuerySet` methods, wired with `Manager.from_queryset(FooQuerySet)()` — note the trailing `()`. It does not live in services or views.
rule.rationale: QuerySet methods chain (`Foo.objects.active().recent()`); a helper in a service does not. Omitting the trailing `()` binds the class instead of an instance, which fails later with a confusing attribute error.

rule.statement: A child model that redefines `objects` MUST replicate the base manager's `alive()` filter, or restate the default explicitly. Silently replacing `objects` is forbidden on a soft-deletable model.
rule.rationale: The most-derived `objects` wins. A child that defines its own manager without the alive filter starts returning soft-deleted rows through every existing call site, and nothing errors.

rule.statement: Every `ForeignKey` and `ManyToManyField` declares `related_name=`. When the reverse accessor is genuinely unwanted, write `related_name="+"`.
rule.rationale: Without it Django derives the reverse name from the model, so two FKs from different models to the same target collide and `makemigrations` fails with a clash error that names neither field usefully.

rule.statement: Custom managers are read-only queryset composers (`.active()`, `.recent()`). A manager method that writes, sends mail, or coordinates a second model (`create_user_send_welcome()`) is forbidden.
rule.rationale: A manager is reachable from every call site including the admin and migrations, so side effects hidden there fire in contexts nobody tested. It is the same defect as logic on the model, one indirection further away.

rule.statement: Add `db_index` (single field) or a `Meta.indexes` composite `Index` for every field combination on a production `filter()` / `order_by()` / `distinct()` path — and only those. Each index is named `appname_model_columns_idx` and carries a justification of at least 10 characters. Drop `db_index=True` where a unique constraint already implies the index.
rule.rationale: A missing composite index turns a list endpoint into a sequential scan at the first customer with real data. An unused one costs an index update on every INSERT and UPDATE forever. Naming makes the index reviewable in the migration diff.

rule.statement: Partial indexes and `UniqueConstraint(condition=Q(...))` are used only when the spec pins `db_engine=postgresql`, with the requirement commented next to the definition.
rule.rationale: The condition is PostgreSQL-specific SQL. On another backend the migration either errors or applies without the condition, so dev and CI end up with different schemas and the divergence surfaces as a flaky integrity error.

rule.statement: Use `select_related` for ForeignKey / OneToOne (a JOIN) and `prefetch_related` for reverse FK and ManyToMany (a second query). Declare them on the QuerySet or Manager for the common access pattern rather than at each call site.
rule.rationale: A per-call `select_related` is forgotten exactly once and the N+1 ships. Attaching it to the manager makes the optimised shape the default and leaves the un-optimised one an explicit choice.

rule.statement: Cross-field invariants go in `clean()`; field-level rules go in `validators=[...]` on the field. Both are inert unless a service calls `full_clean()` (rule r2).
rule.rationale: Neither DRF nor Ninja calls `clean()`. Validation that exists only there is invisible to every API consumer, so it reads as enforced while doing nothing.

rule.statement: Use `db_default` for values the database computes at INSERT (e.g. `Now()`), `default=` for values Python computes, and never both on one field. `GeneratedField` is for columns derived from other columns; pin PostgreSQL when `db_persist=True`.
rule.rationale: `db_default` uses the database clock, which is monotonic across application instances in a way `timezone.now()` in Python is not. `GeneratedField(db_persist=False)` is a virtual column SQLite does not support, so mixing the two produces migrations that only apply on one backend.

rule.statement: A model holding personally identifiable information MUST NOT use `SoftDeleteModel`. PII subject to an erasure request is hard-deleted.
rule.rationale: Soft delete preserves the row by design, which is the opposite of the right to erasure. Marking the model `is_pii` in the spec is what makes the wrong base class a validation failure rather than a legal one.

rule.statement: An app with more than two models replaces `models.py` with a `models/` package — one model per file, re-exported from `models/__init__.py`. `TextChoices` stay in `constants.py`, not in the model files.
rule.rationale: A flat `models.py` is the file every concurrent feature branch touches, so it is where the conflicts land. One file per model also makes the import graph between models visible instead of implicit.

rule.statement: `manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run` runs in pre-commit (see `templates/check-migrations.sh`). Every migration — including a squashed one — is read by a human before `migrate`. An applied migration is never edited; a new one supersedes it.
rule.rationale: A squash can silently drop a partial-index constraint and re-add it without a backfill, which only fails after deploy on rows that already violate it. And a model change without a staged migration is a green CI that breaks the next environment to run `migrate`.
